title: Deep Research
readingMarkdown:
# Deep Research

Ask ChatGPT an ordinary question and you get an answer in seconds, drawn from the model's memory or a quick web search. Switch on **deep research** and something different happens. The system asks you a few clarifying questions, then works alone for anywhere from five minutes to half an hour, running dozens of searches, reading the pages it finds, and returning a structured report of several thousand words with citations. OpenAI launched the feature in February 2025, and every major assistant now has an equivalent.

It is among the most useful things these products do, and among the easiest to misuse, because a long, well-formatted, cited report looks authoritative whether or not it is correct. This chapter teaches both halves of the skill: commissioning good research, and auditing what comes back.

## 1. First-Principles Mental Model & Intuition

### A very fast research intern

Imagine you have an intern who is tireless, reads extremely quickly, and writes well. You give them a question on Monday morning. They ask a couple of sensible clarifying questions, disappear into the library, and return with a neatly formatted memo with footnotes.

You would be pleased. You would not forward that memo to a client unread. An intern, however bright, can misunderstand a source, give a marginal blog the same weight as a government statistic, state something tentative as fact, or attach a footnote to a sentence the footnote does not support. The memo is a strong first draft produced by someone whose judgement you have not yet verified.

That is the correct posture toward a deep research report. It saves hours of searching and reading. It does not save you the job of checking.

### It is an agent

Deep research is the first place in this unit where you meet a real **agent** in the sense of Module 1.6: a model using tools in a loop, deciding its own next step.

```text
   your question
        |
        v
 +----------------+     +--------------------------------------------+
 | CLARIFY        |     |  THE LOOP (runs for minutes)               |
 | asks 2-5       | --> |                                            |
 | questions      |     |   search -> read page -> take notes        |
 +----------------+     |      ^                        |            |
        |               |      |                        v            |
        v               |   decide what is still unknown, search     |
 +----------------+     |   again, follow a link, or stop            |
 | PLAN           | --> |                                            |
 | outline of     |     +----------------------+---------------------+
 | sub-questions  |                            |
 +----------------+                            v
                                   +------------------------+
                                   | SYNTHESISE             |
                                   | write report, attach   |
                                   | citations to claims    |
                                   +------------------------+
```

Every lesson from Module 1.6 applies. Each search-and-read step can go slightly wrong, and errors compound over dozens of steps. The system decides for itself when it has enough, and may stop too early or chase a tangent. And everything it reads on the open web is untrusted text.

### Where the errors come from

There are three distinct places a report can fail, and it helps to keep them apart.

1. **Retrieval.** It found the wrong sources, or missed the important ones.
2. **Reading.** It found a good source and misread it: a wrong number, a dropped "not", a forecast taken as a fact.
3. **Attribution.** It wrote a true or false claim and attached a citation that does not support it.

The third is the most insidious, because the presence of a citation is exactly what makes readers stop checking.

## 2. Core Theory, Mathematical Foundations & Architecture Internals

### What the product does

At the time of writing, a deep research run in ChatGPT follows the pattern in the diagram: clarifying questions, a research plan, an extended period of browsing, and a report with inline citations linked to sources. It can also draw on files you upload. Runs typically take between five and thirty minutes. The number of runs you get per month depends on your plan, and a lighter, cheaper version is used once the full allowance is spent. Allowances have changed several times, so read the counter in the application and ignore figures in older articles.

One detail from OpenAI's developer documentation is worth knowing even if you never use the API: the system consults more sources than it cites. The pages listed in a report's citations are a subset of what was read. A claim can be influenced by a page that never appears in the references.

### OpenAI's own list of limitations

When it launched the feature, OpenAI stated its weaknesses plainly. Deep research can:

- hallucinate facts or make incorrect inferences,
- struggle to distinguish authoritative information from rumours,
- show weak calibration, failing to convey uncertainty accurately,
- make formatting errors in reports and citations.

Keep that list. It is the vendor telling you what to check.

### Independent evidence on citations

Two pieces of outside evidence put numbers on the problem.

**The Tow Center study.** In March 2025, researchers at Columbia University's Tow Center for Digital Journalism tested eight AI search tools. They gave each tool excerpts from news articles and asked it to identify the article, its publisher, and its URL, 200 queries per tool. Overall, more than 60 percent of the responses were incorrect. Tools fabricated links, pointed to syndicated copies instead of the original, and rarely expressed uncertainty. Two cautions apply: the study tested search products, not deep research specifically, and attributing a quoted excerpt is a narrow task. It still shows that a confident citation from an AI system can be wrong more often than it is right.

**DeepResearch Bench.** A 2025 benchmark of 100 doctoral-level research tasks across 22 fields evaluates deep research agents on two axes: the quality of the report, and the accuracy of its citations, meaning whether each cited source really supports the statement it is attached to. Its results showed meaningful differences between products and suggested a trade-off: agents that cite very many sources tend to be less precise about them.

### The probability that a report contains an error

Suppose a report makes $N$ checkable claims and each has an independent probability $e$ of being wrong or unsupported. The expected number of faulty claims is

$$
\mathbb{E}[\text{errors}] = N \times e
$$

and the probability that the report contains at least one is

$$
P(\text{at least one error}) = 1 - (1 - e)^{N}
$$

Take a report with 40 claims and an error rate of only 5 percent per claim. The expected number of errors is 2, and the chance of at least one is $1 - 0.95^{40} \approx 0.87$. A long report from a system that is right 95 percent of the time almost certainly contains a mistake somewhere. This is the same compounding arithmetic as Module 1.6, applied to claims instead of steps. The practical conclusion is that you should assume errors are present and spend your checking effort where an error would matter most.

### Writing a research brief

The quality of a report depends heavily on the request. A deep research run is expensive in time and allowance, so a few minutes on the brief pays back. A complete brief has five parts.

| Part | What to state | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Question | The specific thing you want to know | "How large is the market for refurbished smartphones in India, and how fast is it growing?" |
| Scope | What is in and out | "Consumer sales only. Exclude feature phones and business leasing." |
| Sources | What kinds to prefer or avoid | "Prefer industry analyst reports, company filings, and government data. Avoid vendor marketing pages." |
| Time range | The period that counts | "Data from 2023 onward. State the date of every figure." |
| Deliverable | Format, length, and level of detail | "A two-page summary, a table of market-size estimates with sources, and a list of open questions." |

Three habits improve results further.

- **Answer the clarifying questions properly.** They are the system's attempt to complete your brief. One-word replies waste the run.
- **Replace vague time words.** "Latest" and "recent" mean nothing to a system with no fixed sense of today. Give dates.
- **Ask for uncertainty to be shown.** Request that conflicting figures be presented side by side with their sources, and that the report separate established facts from estimates and from its own inferences.

### Auditing a report

You cannot re-verify every sentence, and you do not need to. Use a triage.

```text
 1. LIST the claims the decision depends on (usually 5 to 10).
 2. For each, OPEN the cited source yourself.
 3. FIND the supporting passage. Does it say what the report says?
        number, unit, date, and direction all matching?
 4. JUDGE the source: who published it, when, and why?
 5. CHECK independence: do several citations trace back to one original?
 6. RECORD the result: supported / partly supported / not found.
```

The fraction of checked claims that are supported is the **citation accuracy** of your sample:

$$
\text{citation accuracy} = \frac{\text{claims supported by their cited source}}{\text{claims checked}}
$$

If you check 10 claims and 7 hold up, treat the rest of the report with corresponding caution. A sample this small has wide uncertainty, as Module 1.8 showed, so its purpose is to tell you roughly whether the report is trustworthy, about 9 in 10 or about 6 in 10, and to make sure the claims that matter most have been read by a person.

**Source quality.** Not all sources deserve equal weight. A rough ordering for factual claims is primary data and official statistics, then peer-reviewed research, then established news organisations and analyst firms, then company marketing and personal blogs, then forums and anonymous posts. Recency matters separately: a 2019 figure quoted as current is an error even if the source is excellent.

**Independence.** Five citations that all repeat one press release are one source, not five. Syndicated news stories and content copied between sites create an illusion of corroboration. Checking whether sources are truly independent is one of the most valuable things a human auditor does, and one of the things automated systems do worst.

**Cost.** A run consumes one of a limited number of monthly allowances and up to half an hour. The audit costs your time: opening and reading ten sources takes perhaps twenty to thirty minutes. Budget for both. A report that nobody had time to check has not saved time. It has deferred a risk.

## 3. Production-Grade Implementation & Annotated Walkthrough

Much of the audit can be supported by code. The following standard-library program checks whether each claim's quoted evidence really appears in the source it cites.

```python
import re

def normalise(text):
    """Lower-case and collapse whitespace so formatting differences do not hide a match."""
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text.lower()).strip()

def check_citations(claims, sources):
    """For each claim, is its quoted evidence present in the source it cites?"""
    results = []
    for claim in claims:
        source_text = sources.get(claim["source_id"])
        if source_text is None:
            results.append("missing_source")
        elif normalise(claim["quote"]) in normalise(source_text):
            results.append("supported")
        else:
            results.append("not_found")
    return results

def citation_accuracy(results):
    return results.count("supported") / len(results) if results else 0.0

sources = {
    "S1": "The refurbished smartphone market in India grew 19 percent in 2024,\n according to the annual survey.",
    "S2": "Analysts expect the segment to reach 12 billion dollars by 2028.",
}
claims = [
    {"text": "The market grew 19% in 2024.", "quote": "grew 19 percent in 2024", "source_id": "S1"},
    {"text": "It will reach 12 billion dollars by 2028.", "quote": "reach 12 billion dollars by 2028", "source_id": "S2"},
    {"text": "It grew 29% in 2024.", "quote": "grew 29 percent in 2024", "source_id": "S1"},
    {"text": "Exports doubled.", "quote": "exports doubled", "source_id": "S9"},
]
results = check_citations(claims, sources)
print(results)
print(f"citation accuracy: {citation_accuracy(results):.2f}")
```

- **`normalise` removes irrelevant differences.** Web pages wrap lines and vary capitalisation. Without normalisation, a genuine quote split across a line break, as in source S1, would be reported as missing.
- **Three outcomes, not two.** A claim whose source cannot be found at all (`missing_source`) is a different problem from one whose source exists and does not contain the quote (`not_found`). The first is often a fabricated or broken link. The second is a misreading or a misattribution.
- **The third claim is the instructive one.** It differs from the first by a single digit, 29 percent instead of 19, and cites the same real source. It is reported as `not_found`. This is exactly the kind of error that survives a casual read, because the sentence is fluent, the citation is real, and only the number is wrong.
- **The check requires a quote.** That is by design. Asking a research tool to supply the exact supporting passage for each key claim converts a vague "trust me" into something a script, or a person, can verify in seconds.
- **Exact matching has limits.** A paraphrased but accurate claim will be reported as not found, and a quote taken out of context ("grew 19 percent" from a sentence saying it did not) will be reported as supported. The tool narrows down where a human needs to look. It does not replace the look.

Two further helpers rate sources and detect duplication.

```python
from urllib.parse import urlparse

def source_score(url, year, current_year=2026):
    """Crude quality score: domain type, minus a point if older than three years."""
    host = urlparse(url).netloc.lower()
    if host.endswith((".gov", ".edu", ".ac.uk", ".gov.in")):
        score = 3
    elif host.endswith(".org"):
        score = 2
    else:
        score = 1
    if current_year - year > 3:
        score -= 1
    return max(score, 0)

def word_set(text):
    return set(re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", text.lower()))

def independent_sources(sources, threshold=0.8):
    """IDs of sources that are not near-duplicates of an earlier one (Jaccard similarity)."""
    kept = []
    for source_id in sorted(sources):
        words = word_set(sources[source_id])
        duplicate = any(
            len(words & word_set(sources[other])) / len(words | word_set(sources[other])) >= threshold
            for other in kept
        )
        if not duplicate:
            kept.append(source_id)
    return kept

print(source_score("https://www.census.gov/data/report", 2025), source_score("https://someblog.example.com/post", 2020))
wire = {"A": "Sales of refurbished phones rose sharply in 2024, the company said on Tuesday.",
        "B": "Sales of refurbished phones rose sharply in 2024, the company said on Tuesday. Read more.",
        "C": "An independent survey of 4,000 buyers found demand was flat."}
print(independent_sources(wire))
```

- **`urlparse(...).netloc` extracts the host.** Testing the whole URL for ".gov" would be fooled by an address such as `example.com/files.gov.pdf`. Checking the end of the host name is the correct test.
- **The score is deliberately crude.** Domain type and age are weak proxies for reliability: there are excellent commercial sources and poor academic ones. A score like this is useful for sorting a long list so that the weakest sources get looked at first. It is not a verdict.
- **`independent_sources` uses Jaccard similarity**, the same measure as in Module 2.4: shared words divided by total distinct words. Sources A and B are the same wire story with two extra words, so B is dropped, and the function reports two independent sources where a naive count would say three.
- **Processing in sorted order makes the result reproducible.** The first of a group of duplicates is kept and the later ones are discarded, so the same input always gives the same output.

**Complexity.** Checking $c$ claims against their sources is linear in the total text length. The duplicate detector compares each source with every kept source, so it is quadratic in the number of sources, which is fine for the tens of sources in a report.

## 4. Practitioner Wisdom & Edge Cases (Reddit / HN / Stack Overflow Synthesis)

**A citation existing is not a citation supporting.** This is the central lesson and the one most often skipped. Click through. Find the sentence. Read the paragraph around it.

**Check numbers, units, and dates above all.** Transposed digits, millions confused with billions, percentages confused with percentage points, and old figures presented as current are the errors that do real damage and that fluent prose hides best.

**Forecasts become facts.** Reports frequently state a projection ("expected to reach") as an outcome ("reached"). Check the tense in the source.

**The system cannot read everything.** Paywalled journals, sites that block automated visitors, scanned documents, and much of the specialist literature are invisible to it. A report can be confidently built on whatever happened to be freely readable. For any serious question, ask yourself what the important sources are and whether they appear.

**Popularity is not authority.** Heavily linked, search-optimised pages are over-represented. A vendor's marketing page and a regulator's dataset may be cited with equal confidence.

**Corroboration can be an illusion.** Several citations repeating one press release, or one statistic copied from site to site without a traceable origin, are a single unverified claim. Trace important figures back to where they were first published.

**A vague brief wastes a scarce run.** Deep research allowances are limited on every plan. People burn them on questions like "tell me about electric vehicles". Decide what you need to know and what you will do with it first.

**Do not connect private data and open browsing carelessly.** A run that can read both your internal files and arbitrary web pages has two legs of the lethal trifecta from Module 1.10. OpenAI's own developer guidance recommends keeping public web research and private data access in separate steps.

**It is weakest where you need it most.** On contested questions, very recent events, and topics with little good public material, the report will still be long, structured, and confident. Length and polish do not vary with the quality of the evidence.

**Use it to get oriented, then read.** Experienced users describe the best use as a fast way to map a topic and find the sources worth reading, followed by reading those sources themselves. Treated that way, it is hard to beat.

## 5. Active Recall Check & Synthesis Summary

**Summary.** Deep research is an agent: it clarifies your question, plans, browses and reads for minutes, and writes a cited report. It can fail at retrieval, at reading, or at attribution, and the vendor itself warns of hallucinated facts, difficulty judging source authority, poor calibration, and citation errors. Because a report makes many claims, even a low per-claim error rate makes at least one error nearly certain. Good results start with a brief that states the question, scope, preferred sources, time range, and deliverable. Good practice ends with an audit: pick the claims that matter, open each cited source, confirm the passage, judge the source, and check that corroborating citations are truly independent. A deep research report is a strong first draft from a fast intern, and it becomes reliable only when a person has checked it.

**Question 1.** A report contains 60 factual claims. If each has a 3 percent chance of being unsupported, compute the expected number of faulty claims and the probability that the report contains at least one. What does this imply about how to spend limited checking time?

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

The expected number of faulty claims is 60 times 0.03, which is 1.8. The probability of at least one is 1 minus 0.97 to the power 60. Since 0.97 to the power 60 is about 0.16, the probability is about 0.84. So even at 97 percent accuracy per claim, the report very probably contains an error. The implication is that you should not ask whether the report has errors, since it almost certainly does, but where an error would be most costly. Identify the handful of claims the decision or the client's conclusion actually rests on and verify those against their sources, with particular attention to numbers, units, and dates.

</details>

**Question 2.** A report supports a key statistic with four citations. On inspection, three are news articles that all quote the same company press release, and the fourth is the press release itself. How many independent sources support the statistic, and what should you do?

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

There is one independent source: the company's press release. The three news articles are syndications or restatements of it and add no independent confirmation. Four citations create an appearance of corroboration that is not real. You should treat the statistic as a single claim made by an interested party, trace it to see whether the press release itself cites underlying data or a methodology, look for a source that measured the same thing independently, such as a regulator, an industry analyst, or a competitor's filing, and report the figure with its true provenance, for example "according to the company" instead of presenting it as established.

</details>

**Question 3.** Rewrite this deep research request as a proper brief with the five parts from Section 2: "What's the latest on AI regulation?"

<details>
<summary>View Answer</summary>

Question: what binding obligations do current laws place on companies that deploy general-purpose AI chat assistants to consumers, and which of those obligations are already in force? Scope: the European Union and the United Kingdom only; laws and binding regulations, not voluntary frameworks or proposals that have not passed; obligations on deployers, not on model developers. Sources: prefer the official legal texts, regulator guidance, and analyses from established law firms; avoid vendor marketing and opinion pieces. Time range: the position as of a stated date, with the date each obligation takes effect and the publication date of every source. Deliverable: a table listing each obligation, its legal basis, its effective date, and its source, followed by a half-page summary and a list of points where sources disagree or the position is uncertain. The original request failed on every part: "latest" is undefined, there was no jurisdiction, no type of regulation, no source preference, and no stated output.

</details>

interactiveLab.labTitle: Hands-On Lab: Build a Research Report Auditor
interactiveLab.context: A consultancy is about to send a client a market report produced with an AI deep research tool, and a partner asks how anyone knows the citations are real. You will build the audit kit: a validator for research briefs, a source-quality scorer, a checker that confirms each quoted claim appears in its cited source, a detector for duplicated sources, and an accuracy score for the report.

steps.title: Validate the research brief
steps.instruction: Implement validate_brief(brief). For every name in REQUIRED_FIELDS that is absent from the dict or blank, add the code 'missing:' followed by the field name. Then, using the provided word_set function on the question, add 'vague:' followed by the word for each word in VAGUE_TIME_WORDS that appears. Return all codes sorted. A deep research run costs minutes and a limited monthly allowance, so the five parts from Section 2 should be in place before you spend one. [MOD-2.7]
steps.hintConceptual: A brief answers five questions: what, within which limits, from which sources, over what period, and delivered how. Words like 'latest' leave the period undefined.
steps.hintSyntax:
problems = [f"missing:{field}" for field in REQUIRED_FIELDS
            if not str(brief.get(field) or "").strip()]
question_words = word_set(str(brief.get("question") or ""))
problems += [f"vague:{word}" for word in VAGUE_TIME_WORDS if word in question_words]
return sorted(problems)
steps.testAssertion:
_bad = validate_brief({"question": "What's the latest on AI regulation?"})
assert _bad == ["missing:deliverable", "missing:scope", "missing:sources", "missing:time_range", "vague:latest"], f"Unexpected result: {_bad}"
_good = {"question": "Which obligations apply to AI chat assistants in the EU?", "scope": "EU only.", "sources": "Official texts.", "time_range": "As of 1 Nov 2026.", "deliverable": "A table."}
assert validate_brief(_good) == [], f"A complete brief has no problems, got {validate_brief(_good)}"
assert validate_brief({}) == ["missing:deliverable", "missing:question", "missing:scope", "missing:sources", "missing:time_range"], "An empty brief is missing all five fields"
assert validate_brief(dict(_good, scope="   ")) == ["missing:scope"], "A blank field counts as missing"
assert validate_brief(dict(_good, question="What are RECENT and current trends in renewable energy?")) == ["vague:current", "vague:recent"], "Vague time words are matched ignoring case and reported sorted"
assert validate_brief(dict(_good, question="How do newspapers cover currents in the Atlantic?")) == [], "Match whole words only: 'newspapers' is not 'new' and 'currents' is not 'current'"
print("Step 1 passed: an incomplete brief is caught before a run is spent on it.")

steps.title: Score a source

Score 3 if the host ends with one of STRONG_SUFFIXES, 2 if it ends with .org, and 1 otherwise. Subtract 1 if the source is more than three years old, and never return less than 0. The score is a rough way to sort a long reference list so that the weakest sources are examined first, following the source-quality ordering in Section 2. [MOD-2.7]

assert source_score("https://example.com/files/report.gov.pdf", 2025) == 1, "'.gov' in the path must not count: check the host only"
assert source_score("https://WWW.MIT.EDU/paper", 2025) == 3, "Host matching must ignore case"
assert source_score("https://a.com/x", 2000, current_year=2010) == 0, "The current_year argument must be respected and the score never goes below 0"
print("Step 2 passed: sources can be sorted so the weakest get checked first.")

steps.title: Check that quotes appear in their sources
steps.instruction: Implement check_citations(claims, sources). For each claim, look up its source_id in the sources dict. If the id is absent, record 'missing_source'. Otherwise compare normalise(quote) with normalise(source text): record 'supported' if the quote is contained in the source and 'not_found' if it is not. Return the statuses in order. This automates step 3 of the audit in Section 2, and it embodies the chapter's main point: a citation existing is not the same as a citation supporting. [MOD-2.7]
steps.hintConceptual: For each claim there are three possibilities: the source cannot be found at all, the source exists and contains the evidence, or the source exists and does not. Normalising both texts stops line breaks and capital letters from hiding a real match.
steps.testAssertion:
_src = {
    "S1": "The refurbished smartphone market in India grew 19 percent in 2024,\n according to the annual survey.",
    "S2": "Analysts expect the segment to reach 12 billion dollars by 2028.",
    "S3": "",
}
_claims = [
    {"quote": "grew 19 percent in 2024", "source_id": "S1"},
    {"quote": "Reach 12 BILLION dollars by 2028", "source_id": "S2"},
    {"quote": "grew 29 percent in 2024", "source_id": "S1"},
    {"quote": "exports doubled", "source_id": "S9"},
    {"quote": "in 2024, according to the annual survey", "source_id": "S1"},
    {"quote": "anything", "source_id": "S3"},
]
assert check_citations(_claims, _src) == ["supported", "supported", "not_found", "missing_source", "supported", "not_found"], f"Unexpected statuses: {check_citations(_claims, _src)}"
assert check_citations([], _src) == [], "No claims gives an empty list"
assert check_citations([{"quote": "grew 19 percent", "source_id": "S2"}], _src) == ["not_found"], "A real quote attributed to the WRONG source is not supported"
print("Step 3 passed: a one-digit change (19 to 29) with a real citation is caught.")

steps.title: Compute citation accuracy
steps.instruction: Implement citation_accuracy(statuses). Return the number of statuses equal to 'supported' divided by the total number of statuses, or 0.0 for an empty list. This is the formula from Section 2. Applied to a sample of a report's key claims, it tells you roughly how far to trust the rest. [MOD-2.7]
steps.hintConceptual: It is a simple fraction: of the claims you checked, how many held up. Both 'not found' and 'missing source' count against the report.
steps.testAssertion:
assert citation_accuracy(["supported", "supported", "not_found", "missing_source"]) == 0.5, "2 supported out of 4 is 0.5"
assert citation_accuracy(["supported"] * 7 + ["not_found"] * 3) == 0.7, "7 supported out of 10 is 0.7"
assert citation_accuracy(["not_found", "missing_source"]) == 0.0, "No supported claims gives 0.0"
assert citation_accuracy(["supported", "supported"]) == 1.0, "All supported gives 1.0"
assert citation_accuracy([]) == 0.0, "An empty list gives 0.0, not an error"
assert isinstance(citation_accuracy(["supported"]), float), "The result must be a float"
print("Step 4 passed: the report now has a measured citation accuracy.")

steps.title: Find the truly independent sources
steps.instruction: Implement independent_sources(sources, threshold). Go through the source ids in sorted order. For each, compute the Jaccard similarity between its word set and the word set of every id already kept: the size of the intersection divided by the size of the union. If any similarity is at or above the threshold, the source is a near-duplicate and is skipped; otherwise add its id to the kept list. Return the kept ids. Several citations of one press release are one source, and this is how to count them honestly. [MOD-2.7]
steps.hintConceptual: Corroboration only counts when the sources are independent. Texts that share nearly all their words are copies of each other, so keep the first and discard the rest.
steps.testAssertion:
_wire = {
    "A": "Sales of refurbished phones rose sharply in 2024, the company said on Tuesday.",
    "B": "Sales of refurbished phones rose sharply in 2024, the company said on Tuesday. Read more.",
    "C": "An independent survey of 4,000 buyers found demand was flat.",
}
assert independent_sources(_wire) == ["A", "C"], f"B is a near-copy of A, so only A and C are independent, got {independent_sources(_wire)}"
assert independent_sources({"x": "one two three", "y": "four five six"}) == ["x", "y"], "Texts with no shared words are independent"
assert independent_sources({"b": "same words here", "a": "same words here", "c": "same words here"}) == ["a"], "Identical texts collapse to the first id in sorted order"
assert independent_sources({}) == [], "No sources gives an empty list"
assert independent_sources(_wire, threshold=0.99) == ["A", "B", "C"], "With a very strict threshold A and B are no longer treated as duplicates"
assert independent_sources({"p": "alpha beta gamma delta", "q": "alpha beta gamma epsilon"}, threshold=0.6) == ["p"], "Jaccard 3/5 = 0.6 meets a threshold of 0.6"
print("Step 5 passed: three citations, two independent sources.")
